description: A group of four physicists and developers united by a shared passion for science and technology, and a common goal of putting our skills to the test by developing engaging solutions.
summary:
Earth Trends Nexus is a free web app that turns decades of NASA Earth science data into clear answers about how a place is changing. Users pick any point on an interactive globe, and the app downloads monthly NASA POWER records (MERRA-2 and CERES, 1981 to today) for 20 variables, from temperature and rainfall to soil moisture, aerosols and ozone. It tests every variable at once with the Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope and an autocorrelation-corrected t-test, then ranks the strongest trends and grades the evidence in plain language. Users can see when in the year the change happens, compare it with the surrounding region and other places, and confirm it in NASA Giovanni. At 17 featured places, OMI, AIRS, GLDAS and MERRA-2 aerosol records add air-quality and water-cycle variables, and users can import their own time series.

The app covers the whole challenge in one tool: choosing variables, getting the data, plotting long time series and testing whether the trends are significant. This matters because students, teachers, journalists and decision-makers can replace impressions with evidence about climate change where they live, without coding or specialist software.
details:
Link for GitHub repository: https://github.com/nicholas1301/earth-trends-explorer

What does it do and how does it work?

Earth Trends Nexus is a free web app. It lets anyone pick a place on Earth and find out what is changing there, how fast, when in the year, how widely, and whether the change is statistically significant.

The investigation runs in four steps:

  1. Pick a place. Click anywhere on an interactive globe or Equal Earth map, search for a place, or choose one of 17 featured places. These include Svalbard, the Aral Sea, the Sahel, Manaus, Delhi and the Antarctic Peninsula.
    • the Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope
    • an OLS regression with a t-test that corrects for autocorrelation, which stops neighbouring years from overstating the result
  2. Where is it changing? A regional grid map shows whether the trend is local or part of a wider pattern. A world comparison ranks the place against others. This matters because the same process can push a variable up in one region and down in another.

Going beyond NASA POWER:

  • Each variable has a link that opens NASA Giovanni already filled in with the same place and period. Giovanni gives access to MODIS, OMI, AIRS, GPM IMERG and GLDAS.
    • OMI nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and UV index
    • AIRS heat escaping to space and cloud-top temperature
    • GLDAS runoff, deep soil water and water stored in snow
    • MERRA-2 fine particles (PM2.5), dust and soot

They are tested exactly like the others. This adds air-quality and water-cycle questions to the investigation, such as whether NO₂ is rising in Delhi or the ground is drying out in the Murray-Darling basin. MODIS records of vegetation, tree cover, fires and land surface temperature are being added next.

Guided demo cases and challenges teach users how to investigate. Examples are “Is the Arctic warming?”, “Has the rain returned to the Sahel?” and “Hot days or warm nights in São Paulo?”.

What benefits does it have?

  • No installation, account or coding needed. It works in any browser, on a computer or a phone.
  • It does the whole job in one place. Data sites can make time series and statistics packages can test significance, but this app selects the variables, gets the data, plots it and tests it together.
  • It helps you choose variables. Because every variable is tested and ranked automatically, users no longer have to guess which variables to look at, which the challenge describes as a key difficulty.
  • The statistics are honest. Two tests are used, autocorrelation is corrected, and evidence is graded in plain language instead of a bare p-value. The app also warns when a record is too short for a reliable trend.
  • It is transparent and reproducible. Users can export results as CSV, share an investigation by link, see the source of each variable, and cross-check results against independent NASA records.

Intended impact

We want to make NASA Earth science data understandable and usable by students, teachers, journalists, local decision-makers and curious citizens, not only by specialists. Users can turn “I think it’s getting hotter here” into “air temperature is rising 0.4 °C per decade, mostly in winter, and the result is very significant.” The goal is to replace impressions with evidence-based conclusions about climate and environmental change where people live. The app also teaches good scientific habits along the way: checking significance, comparing with independent records, and asking whether a change is local or regional.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, plus JavaScript for the data scripts (Node.js), HTML and CSS
  • Framework and build: React 18 and Vite. Unit tests use Vitest.
  • Charts and maps: made by hand as SVG React components, with no chart library. d3-geo provides the orthographic globe and Equal Earth projections. Coastlines come from Natural Earth via world-atlas and topojson-client.
  • Statistics: our own code for Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope, OLS, and the t and normal distributions, all unit tested
  • Data: the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2 and CERES), plus NASA Giovanni (OMI, AIRS, GLDAS and MERRA-2 aerosols). Users can also import files from NASA AppEEARS, KNMI Climate Explorer and NOAA Climate Data Online.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages with automatic deployment through GitHub Actions
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop. No special hardware was needed.

How is the project creative?

  • It is framed as a detective story. You pick a place, look at the trends, weigh the evidence, then check where else it is happening. This makes statistical analysis feel like solving a mystery.
  • Every variable is scanned at once, so the data shows you what is changing instead of you having to guess.
  • Users can bring their own data. Exports from four different services can be analysed in the same app, and nothing leaves the browser.
  • It has guided cases and challenges that teach how to interpret results, for example how a shorter period can change the verdict on the Sahel’s rain.
  • It has a clear visual identity inspired by the Space Apps logo, with light and dark modes and an interactive globe that animates to each place.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific rigour vs. accessibility: we used robust, non-parametric tests and corrected for autocorrelation, but explained results in plain language with graded levels of evidence.
  • Data coverage: NASA POWER has no MODIS, OMI, AIRS, GPM or GLDAS data. We closed that gap with Giovanni links, imported files and records stored in the project. We also assessed every recommended challenge resource and documented which ones we integrated and why.
  • Technical limits: some NASA services, such as Giovanni, cannot be queried directly from a web page. So the records for the featured places were downloaded ahead of time and ship with the app, and they load instantly.
  • Performance: each place’s data is fetched once and cached. Changing filters, seasons or periods recalculates results instantly without downloading again.
  • Record length and statistical pitfalls: we used 40+ years of data and warn when a series is too short, using the SWOT mission as the example.
  • Privacy: imported files stay on the user’s device.
  • Usability and access: the app is a free static site that works on phones, needs nothing installed, and offers dark mode and a help dialog.
